claims.source: mGluR2-R57A displayed very similar responses to LY48 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E) and the LY48 dose–response curves for mGluR2-WT and mGluR2-R57A were identical with both showing maximal PAM-induced activation of ~70% relative to glutamate and an EC50 of ~300 nM (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: Co-application of a saturating concentration of LY341495 (LY34), a competitive antagonist that prevents LBD closure, did not prevent mGluR2 activation by LY48.
claims.source: Co-application of a saturating concentration of LY341495 (LY34), a competitive antagonist that prevents LBD closure (Vafabakhsh et al., 2015) did not prevent mGluR2 activation by LY48 (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1D and a citation to Vafabakhsh et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Complete removal of the extracellular domain did not prevent LY48-mediated activation.
claims.source: Furthermore, consistent with previous studies (El Moustaine et al., 2012), complete removal of the extracellular domain did not prevent LY48-mediated activation, indicating that an intact LBD is not needed for mGluR2 activation (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1E and a citation to El Moustaine et al., 2012.

claims.claim: Saturating concentrations of LY48 were unable to directly induce LBD closure as assayed using an inter-LBD FRET assay.
claims.source: Despite the modulatory effects of the LBD on PAM activation, saturating concentrations of LY48 were unable to directly induce LBD closure as assayed using an inter-LBD FRET assay (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: SNAP-mGluR2 molecules photobleached primarily in one-step (~40%) or two-step (~60%) events with a small population showing >3 steps (5.5 ± 0.61%).
claims.source: Consistent with previous studies, following immobilization with a biotinylated anti-HA antibody, single SNAP-mGluR2 molecules photobleached primarily in one-step (~40%) or two-step (~60%) events with a small population showing >3 steps (5.5 ± 0.61%) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C), consistent with an obligatory dimer with ~80% SNAP labeling efficiency (Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by single-molecule pulldown data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C.

claims.claim: SNAP-mGluR2-TMD displayed ~45% of spots bleaching in 2-steps, consistent with a population of ~60% dimers.
claims.source: We next performed the same measurements with SNAP-mGluR2-TMD and observed ~45% of spots bleaching in 2-steps (Figure 2B–D), consistent with a population of ~60% dimers.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by single-molecule pulldown data shown in Figure 2B–D.

claims.claim: SNAP-mGluR1-TMD, SNAP-mGluR3-TMD and SNAP-mGluR5-TMD all exhibited a lower two-step photobleaching frequency (~30%) compared to SNAP-mGluR2-TMD.
claims.source: Compared to SNAP-mGluR2-TMD, SNAP-mGluR1-TMD, SNAP-mGluR3-TMD and SNAP-mGluR5-TMD all exhibited a lower two-step photobleaching frequency (~30%) (Figure 2D; Figure 2—figure supplement 2), which suggests that the strength and extent of inter-TMD interaction is mGluR subtype-specific.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by single-molecule pulldown data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: SNAP-ß2AR showed ~10% two-step photobleaching which is consistent with a pure monomer.
claims.source: We expressed HA- and SNAP-tagged ß2AR ('SNAP-ß2AR') and pulled down surface receptors from HEK 293T cell lysate via the same anti-HA antibody and under identical lysis conditions to the mGluRs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2). We observed ~10% two-step photobleaching which is consistent with a pure monomer (Materials and methods) (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by single-molecule pulldown data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Application of PAMs or NAMs to SNAP-mGluR2-TMD did not alter the photobleaching step distributions.
claims.source: We counted SNAP-mGluR2-TMD bleaching steps in the presence of either two different mGluR2 PAMs (LY48 and BINA) or two different mGluR2 NAMs (MNI 137 and Ro 64–2259) and found that the photobleaching step distributions in all cases were similar, with ~40–45% two-step bleaching events (Figure 2E,F; Figure 2—figure supplement 3A) and no change in the proportion of higher order complexes with >3 bleaching steps (<10%).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by single-molecule pulldown data shown in Figure 2E,F and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claims.claim: Application of LY48 to SNAP-mGluR2-TMD and CLIP-mGluR2-TMD produced a readily detectable FRET increase, which was reversed with drug washout.
claims.source: Strikingly, application of LY48 produced a readily detectable FRET increase, as determined by a simultaneous increase in acceptor fluorescence and decrease in donor fluorescence, which was reversed with drug washout (Figure 3B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: LY48-induced FRET responses were repeatable, showed no desensitization over 5 min, were blocked by the NAM MNI 137 and dose-dependent over the concentration range used for functional experiments.
claims.source: LY48-induced FRET responses were repeatable (Figure 3C), showed no desensitization over 5 min (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), were blocked by the NAM MNI 137 (Figure 3D) and dose-dependent over the concentration range used for functional experiments (Figure 3E,F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, Figure 3D, and Figure 3E,F.

claims.claim: Application of the mGluR5 PAM VU0360172 to SNAP-mGluR5-TMD produced a reversible FRET response.
claims.source: To test if LBD-independent inter-TMD rearrangement is a feature of other mGluRs, we asked if donor and acceptor conjugation to SNAP-mGluR5-TMD would allow for the detection a FRET response to a PAM. Application of the mGluR5 PAM VU0360172 produced a reversible FRET response suggesting that, indeed, this conformational assay is generalizable across the mGluR family (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claims.claim: Co-expression of a dominant-negative Gα protein resulted in a substantial left-shift in the inter-TMD FRET dose–response curve.
claims.source: Consistent with this model, when we co-expressed a dominant-negative Gα protein with reduced guanine nucleotide affinity to stabilize the receptor–G protein interaction (Barren and Artemyev, 2007), there was a substantial left-shift in the inter-TMD FRET dose–response curve (Figure 3F; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2, and a citation to Barren and Artemyev, 2007.

claims.claim: Mutation of asparagine 735 to aspartate (N735D) resulted in drastically reduced activation by LY48 in the GIRK assay.
claims.source: Consistent with our prediction, mutation of asparagine 735 to aspartate (N735D) resulted in drastically reduced activation by LY48 in the GIRK assay (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B,C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B,C.

claims.claim: The N735D mutant showed a ~ 20 fold rightward shift in the LY48 inter-TMD FRET dose–response curve compared to the wild-type receptor.
claims.source: Consistent with functional measurements, the N735D mutant showed a ~ 20 fold rightward shift in the LY48 inter-TMD FRET dose–response curve compared to the wild-type receptor (Figure 3—figure supplement 3D,E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3D,E.

claims.claim: All the PAMs tested produced a clear, dose-dependent increase in inter-TMD FRET.
claims.source: Similar to LY48, all the PAMs tested produced a clear, dose-dependent increase in inter-TMD FRET (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B.

claims.claim: At saturating concentrations, the PAMs produced different maximal FRET changes, as compared to saturating LY48.
claims.source: At saturating concentrations, however, the PAMs produced different maximal FRET changes, as compared to saturating LY48 (Figure 4C; Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: TASP 0433864 produced a maximum FRET increase of ~1.3 times that of LY48, whereas BINA produced an increase only ~0.8 times that of LY48.
claims.source: TASP 0433864 produced a maximum FRET increase of ~1.3 times that of LY48, whereas BINA produced an increase only ~0.8 times that of LY48.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FRET data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: There was no correlation between the apparent PAM affinity and the apparent efficacy, as measured by maximal TMD FRET change.
claims.source: Importantly, there was no correlation between the apparent PAM affinity and the apparent efficacy, as measured by maximal TMD FRET change (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: All the tested PAMs modulated the DCG-IV response, but did not alter LBD FRET in the absence of an orthosteric agonist.
claims.source: Similar to LY48, all the tested PAMs modulated the DCG-IV response, but did not alter LBD FRET in the absence of an orthosteric agonist (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claims.claim: The maximal inter-TMD FRET change produced by a given PAM is correlated with its ability to both modulate the agonist response and to directly produce G-protein activation.
claims.source: Strikingly, the maximal inter-TMD FRET change produced by a given PAM is correlated with its ability to both modulate the agonist response (Figure 4I; Figure 4—figure supplement 3B) and to directly produce G-protein activation (Figure 4J; Figure 4—figure supplement 3C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FRET and functional data shown in Figure 4I, Figure 4J, Figure 4—figure supplement 3B, and Figure 4—figure supplement 3C.

claims.claim: Xanthurenic acid (XA) did not produce inter-TMD FRET changes or GIRK currents in full-length mGluR2-expressing cells at concentrations up to 50 µM.
claims.source: We applied XA at concentrations up to 50 µM and observed neither inter-TMD FRET changes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A) nor GIRK currents in full-length mGluR2-expressing cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FRET and electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,B.

claims.claim: Across all concentrations, both the induction and the reversal of inter-LBD FRET in response to glutamate was faster than the PAM-induced changes.
claims.source: Across all concentrations, both the induction and the reversal of inter-LBD FRET in response to glutamate was faster than the PAM-induced changes (Figure 5B,C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 5B,C.

claims.claim: Saturating LY48-induced GIRK currents were significantly slower than saturating glutamate-induced GIRK currents.
claims.source: Indeed, saturating LY48-induced GIRK currents were significantly slower than saturating glutamate-induced GIRK currents (10 µM LY48 (time 10% to 90%)=14.3 ± 3.5 s versus 1 mM Glutamate (Time 10% to 90%)=1.9 ± 0.5 s; paired T-test, p=0.04).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data and statistical analysis presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: BINA showed drastically slower FRET responses that took up to 3 min to reach a steady state and were irreversible on the time scale of measurements for up to 10 min.
claims.source: To our surprise, while saturating concentrations of LY48, CBiPES, and TASP gave rise to clear FRET responses with relatively rapid onset (10–40 s) and reversal (<2 min), BINA showed drastically slower FRET responses that took up to 3 min to reach a steady state and were irreversible on the time scale of our measurements for up to 10 min (Figure 6A,B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claims.claim: LY48 showed fully-reversible currents, whereas BINA responses were maintained following up to 10 min of washout in the GIRK activation assay.
claims.source: These distinct kinetics of PAM responses were maintained in our GIRK activation assay where LY48 showed fully-reversible currents, whereas BINA responses were maintained following up to 10 min of washout (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: MNI 137 clearly reversed the BINA-induced FRET increase back to baseline.
claims.source: MNI 137 clearly reversed the BINA-induced FRET increase back to baseline, implying that it indeed can rapidly compete with BINA for a common binding site (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: Following washout of MNI 137 a slow FRET increase was observed even though BINA was not reapplied.
claims.source: However, following washout of MNI 137 a slow FRET increase was observed even though BINA was not reapplied.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FRET data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Of the four PAMs tested, BINA produced the greatest changes in gramicidin channel function (i.e. membrane properties) over a range of concentrations from 1 to 10 µM.
claims.source: Of the four PAMs tested, BINA produced the greatest changes in gramicidin channel function (i.e. membrane properties) over a range of concentrations from 1 to 10 µM (Figure 6—figure supplement 3B,C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data from the gramicidin-based fluorescence assay shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3B,C.

claims.claim: Application of MNI 137 alone produced minimal FRET changes even at the highest concentrations tested.
claims.source: Application of MNI 137 alone produced minimal FRET changes even at the highest concentrations tested (Figure 6B), suggesting that the resting TMD conformation is not altered, though our sensors may not detect very localized conformational changes.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 6B (note: this should be Figure 7B based on the manuscript structure).

claims.claim: Ro 64–5229 produced robust, dose-dependent inter-TMD FRET increases with amplitudes comparable to mGluR2 PAMs.
claims.source: In contrast, Ro 64–5229 ('Ro 64') produced robust, dose-dependent inter-TMD FRET increases with amplitudes comparable to mGluR2 PAMs (Figure 7B,C; Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 7B,C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Ro 64 showed similar ON kinetics to LY48, but very slow OFF kinetics that did not fully reverse on the time course of experiments.
claims.source: Interestingly, Ro 64 showed similar ON kinetics to LY48 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B), but very slow OFF kinetics that did not fully reverse on the time course of our experiments (Figure 7B; Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Neither MNI 137 nor Ro 64 produced changes in gramicidin channel function indicating that they do not alter membrane properties.
claims.source: However, unlike BINA, neither MNI 137 nor Ro 64 produced changes in gramicidin channel function indicating that they do not alter membrane properties (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C), despite their hydrophobicity (cLogP ≈ 1.7 for MNI 137 and ≈ 4.9 for Ro 64).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data from the gramicidin-based fluorescence assay shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Saturating concentrations of either MNI 137 or Ro 64 showed a similar level of partial antagonism of the FRET response to DCG-IV.
claims.source: Saturating concentrations of either MNI 137 or Ro 64 showed a similar level of partial antagonism of the FRET response to DCG-IV (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D–F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D–F.

claims.claim: MNI 137 showed no effect on basal current in cells expressing GIRK and full-length mGluR2.
claims.source: Whereas MNI 137 showed no effect on basal current (Figure 7D), Ro 64 produced a small but clear outward current (Figure 7E,F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: Ro 64 produced a small but clear outward current in cells expressing GIRK and full-length mGluR2.
claims.source: Whereas MNI 137 showed no effect on basal current (Figure 7D), Ro 64 produced a small but clear outward current (Figure 7E,F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 7E,F.

claims.claim: Ro 64 acts as an inverse agonist while MNI 137 is a neutral antagonist.
claims.source: These data show that Ro 64 acts as an inverse agonist while MNI 137 is a neutral antagonist.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the functional data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Ro 64 did not alter the basal inter-LBD FRET, indicating that it exerts its effects without altering LBD conformation.
claims.source: Despite the effect on basal GIRK activity, Ro 64 did not alter the basal inter-LBD FRET, indicating that it exerts its effects without altering LBD conformation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1G), as is also seen with MNI 137 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1H).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1G,H.

claims.claim: MNI 137 was able to partially reverse the inter-TMD FRET increase induced by Ro 64.
claims.source: Consistent with Ro 64 serving as an inverse agonist and MNI 137 serving as a neutral antagonist, MNI 137 was able to partially reverse the inter-TMD FRET increase induced by Ro 64 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1I).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1I.

results.result: PAMs directly activate mGluR2 independently of the LBD. LY48 produces large, reversible GIRK currents (~70% of glutamate response) that are blocked by NAMs, occur in glutamate-insensitive mutants, persist when LBD closure is prevented by competitive antagonists, and occur in isolated TMDs lacking the extracellular domain. PAMs do not induce LBD closure.
results.evaluation: Claims C11, C15-C20 provide converging evidence from multiple experimental approaches (GIRK activation, mutant analysis, competitive antagonism, domain deletion, FRET) demonstrating that PAMs can activate mGluR2 through the TMD independently of LBD conformational changes. The data are internally consistent and supported by appropriate controls.

results.result: mGluR2 TMDs show enhanced dimerization propensity compared to other mGluRs and class A GPCRs. Single-molecule photobleaching reveals ~60% dimers for mGluR2-TMD versus ~40% for mGluR1/3/5-TMDs and ~10% for β2AR. TMD dimerization is insensitive to PAM or NAM application.
results.evaluation: Claims C12, C21-C25 demonstrate subtype-specific TMD dimerization using single-molecule subunit counting with appropriate controls. The photobleaching step distributions are consistent with the proposed stoichiometries given the stated labeling efficiency (~80%). The lack of ligand-induced changes in stoichiometry supports the interpretation that conformational rearrangement rather than assembly/disassembly occurs upon activation.

results.result: A novel inter-TMD FRET assay reveals LBD-independent, reversible conformational rearrangements upon PAM binding. The FRET response is repeatable, non-desensitizing, blocked by NAMs, dose-dependent, enhanced by dominant-negative G-protein, and depends on the N735 'trigger switch' residue.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C26-C31 establish a new conformational assay with appropriate controls demonstrating that it reports on functionally relevant TMD rearrangements. The correlation with functional measurements (GIRK activation), sensitivity to known mechanistic mutations (N735D), and modulation by G-protein coupling all support the validity of the assay. The assay is generalizable to mGluR5 (C28).

results.result: Different PAMs show variable efficacy, affinity, and functional effects. PAMs produce different maximal inter-TMD FRET changes (TASP ~1.3x, BINA ~0.8x relative to LY48) with no correlation between affinity and efficacy. Maximal inter-TMD FRET correlates with both allosteric modulation of agonist responses and direct G-protein activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C13, C32-C37 demonstrate pharmacological diversity among PAMs using the inter-TMD FRET assay. The correlations between inter-TMD FRET efficacy and both functional readouts (modulation and activation) are compelling and suggest the assay reports on a physiologically relevant conformational state. The lack of correlation between affinity and efficacy is an important pharmacological observation.

results.result: Xanthurenic acid (XA) does not act as an mGluR2 PAM. No inter-TMD FRET changes or GIRK currents were observed at concentrations up to 50 μM.
results.evaluation: Claim C38 provides negative data using two independent assays (FRET and GIRK) at concentrations well above those previously reported for XA activity. This addresses a controversial claim in the literature and demonstrates the utility of the inter-TMD FRET assay for drug screening.

results.result: PAM-induced responses show distinct kinetics compared to glutamate and between different PAMs. Glutamate-induced inter-LBD FRET changes are faster than LY48-induced inter-TMD FRET changes. BINA shows drastically slower kinetics (3 min to steady state) and irreversibility compared to other PAMs.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C42 demonstrate kinetic heterogeneity among PAMs using both FRET and GIRK assays. The slower kinetics of PAMs versus glutamate and the dramatic differences between BINA and other PAMs are clearly documented. Statistical significance is provided for key comparisons (C40).

results.result: BINA's slow kinetics and irreversibility are attributed to membrane partitioning. MNI 137 reverses BINA-induced FRET, but FRET increases again after NAM washout without BINA reapplication. BINA produces the greatest changes in membrane properties in a gramicidin-based assay.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C45 provide a mechanistic explanation for BINA's unique kinetic profile. The gramicidin assay provides independent evidence for membrane interaction. The observation that MNI 137 can reverse BINA effects but that FRET returns after NAM washout supports a membrane reservoir model. However, alternative explanations (e.g., different binding sites) are not fully excluded.

results.result: NAMs show distinct mechanisms: MNI 137 is a neutral antagonist while Ro 64 is an inverse agonist. MNI 137 produces minimal inter-TMD FRET changes and no basal GIRK current changes. Ro 64 produces robust inter-TMD FRET increases, slow OFF kinetics, and small outward GIRK currents. Both NAMs partially antagonize agonist responses and do not alter LBD conformation.
results.evaluation: Claims C14, C46-C55 comprehensively characterize two NAMs using multiple assays (inter-TMD FRET, GIRK, inter-LBD FRET, gramicidin). The classification of Ro 64 as an inverse agonist is supported by the observation of outward GIRK currents (C52) and inter-TMD FRET increases (C47) in the absence of agonist. The distinction from MNI 137 is clear and well-documented.

results.result: A three-state model of TMD activation is proposed where PAMs and inverse agonists stabilize different high-FRET states, while neutral antagonists stabilize a low-FRET resting state.
results.evaluation: Claims C3 and C53, supported by the data showing that both PAMs (C26-C27, C32) and the inverse agonist Ro 64 (C47) increase inter-TMD FRET while the neutral antagonist MNI 137 does not (C46), provide evidence for at least three distinct conformational states. The model is consistent with all experimental observations, though the structural basis requires further investigation.

results.result: Background and context claims about mGluR structure, function, dimerization, and prior work on PAMs and TMD activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C4-C10 provide established background information supported by appropriate citations to prior literature. These claims accurately represent the current state of knowledge and provide context for the current work.
